body:
Foundation and contributors

Kumar is a Gujarati cultural and literary monthly that began publication in Ahmedabad in January 1924. It was founded by the distinguished Gujarati artist and art educator Ravishankar Raval.

Raval recognised that young Gujarati readers needed a publication capable of developing their understanding of literature, art, science and culture. Kumar was created to address this educational need.

Bachubhai Rawat, a writer, editor and printing enthusiast, collaborated closely with Raval in developing the journal. He subsequently played a major role in its editorial and publication activities.

Meaning and intended readership

The name Kumar refers to youth. The magazine's early identity reflected its intention to educate the younger and emerging literate generation of Gujarati society.

However, it was not simply a children's entertainment magazine. It offered informative and literary material intended to develop curiosity, creativity, cultural awareness and intellectual interests.

Major areas of content

  • Literature: Poems, short stories, essays and other creative writing.
  • Visual arts: Paintings, illustrations and explanations of artistic ideas.
  • Science and general knowledge: Informative articles on scientific and educational subjects.
  • Culture: Discussion of Indian and Gujarati artistic and cultural traditions.
  • Personal development: Material intended to cultivate useful skills and an informed outlook among young readers.

Contribution to Gujarati culture

Kumar helped bring visual art and literary culture into the everyday reading experience of Gujarati audiences. Its illustrated format demonstrated that a Gujarati periodical could communicate ideas through both written material and visual representation.

Its broad educational character is an important distinguishing feature. Buddhiprakash emerged from the 19th-century movement for knowledge and social reform, while Kumar developed in the 20th century with a particular emphasis on the literary, artistic and intellectual development of younger readers.

Remember the principal association

Kumar is particularly associated with Ravishankar Raval and Bachubhai Rawat. Ravishankar Raval's identity as an artist explains the magazine's distinctive emphasis on visual art and cultural education.

Prelims focus

  • First publication: January 1924.
  • Place of origin: Ahmedabad.
  • Founder and first editor: Ravishankar Raval.
  • Important collaborator and later editor: Bachubhai Rawat.
  • Nature: Illustrated Gujarati cultural and literary monthly.
  • Trap: Kumar was not founded by Mahatma Gandhi or Indulal Yagnik.

[References: Gujarati Vishwakosh, Kumar, and Bachubhai Rawat; Vasvi Oza, Readers Write: Translating Modern Art Debate in Gujarati Periodical Kumar, artVarta Research Grant 2021, Akar Prakar; Vasvi Oza, Tracing Ravishankar Raval's Art Pedagogy in the Gujarati Periodical Kumar, Critical Collective. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Kumar combined literary education with artistic and cultural awareness.

title: Kumar: Art, Literature and Education through Gujarati Journalism

body:
Origin under Indulal Yagnik

Navjivan, also written as Navajivan, is closely associated with Mahatma Gandhi and the Indian national movement. However, its origins precede Gandhi's editorship.

In 1915, Indulal Kanaiyalal Yagnik started a Gujarati monthly called Navjivan ane Satya in Bombay. The publication discussed education, social questions and public life in Gujarat.

Indulal Yagnik subsequently entrusted the publication to Mahatma Gandhi in 1919. Under Gandhi's leadership, it was renamed Navjivan and converted into a weekly journal.

The first issue of Navjivan under Gandhi's editorship appeared on 7 September 1919 from Ahmedabad.

Navjivan under Mahatma Gandhi

Gandhi regarded journalism as an instrument of public education and social transformation. Through Navjivan, he could communicate directly with Gujarati-speaking readers and explain the principles underlying the national movement.

Important themes included:

  • Swaraj: Self-rule and the responsibilities associated with freedom.
  • Satyagraha: Resistance to injustice through truth and non-violent action.
  • Swadeshi: Encouragement of indigenous production and consumption.
  • Social reform: Removal of untouchability, improvement of social conditions and constructive work.
  • Public education: Encouraging informed participation in national and community life.

Comparison with Young India

Gandhi used both Gujarati and English journalism to communicate with different groups of readers. Navjivan and Young India were important publications associated with this effort.

FeatureNavjivanYoung India
Principal languageGujaratiEnglish
Frequency under GandhiWeeklyWeekly
Important associationMahatma Gandhi and Indulal YagnikMahatma Gandhi
Gandhi's autobiographyGujarati originalEnglish translation

A Hindi edition of Navajivan was also introduced in 1921. Therefore, the description of Navjivan as a Gujarati weekly refers specifically to its original Gujarati edition under Gandhi.

Publication of Gandhi's autobiography

Gandhi originally wrote his autobiography in Gujarati under the title Satya na Prayogo athva Atmakatha.

It appeared in successive instalments in Navjivan from 29 November 1925 to 3 February 1929. Its English translation, known as The Story of My Experiments with Truth, appeared in Young India.

This connection makes Navjivan important not only in the history of political journalism but also in the history of Gujarati autobiographical literature.

Prelims focus

  • Navjivan ane Satya: Gujarati monthly started by Indulal Yagnik in 1915.
  • First Navjivan issue under Gandhi: 7 September 1919, Ahmedabad.
  • Navjivan was a Gujarati weekly under Gandhi.
  • Young India was an English weekly.
  • Gandhi's Gujarati autobiography was serialised in Navjivan during 1925–1929.
  • Trap: Gandhi took over an existing publication; he was not the original founder of Navjivan ane Satya.

[References: Ramesh Malabhai Chauhan, Gujarat's First Educational Conference: A Study, Towards Excellence, Gujarat University, Vol. 13, Issue 2, June 2021, p. 700, reference 11; Gandhi Heritage Portal, Navajivan, Vol. 1, Issue 1, 7 September 1919, and Hindi Navajivan archive; National Digital Library of India, Navajivan, Vol. 1, Issue 9, 2 November 1919; MKGandhi.org, Gandhi's Journals: How the Mahatma Shaped a Nation's Ideas through Young India, Navjivan and Harijan; Press Information Bureau, Government of India, Gandhi Heritage Portal launch release, 2 September 2013. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Navjivan developed from a Gujarati monthly into a major Gandhian weekly.

title: Navjivan: Gandhian Journalism and National Awakening

body:
Meaning of a public library movement

A public library movement seeks to make books, newspapers and other reading material accessible to ordinary people. Unlike a private collection maintained for an individual or family, a public library serves the educational and informational needs of a wider community.

The development of public libraries was particularly important during the colonial period because many people could not afford to purchase books. Libraries made it possible for several readers to use the same collection and helped extend education beyond schools and colleges.

Role of Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III

The princely state of Baroda became a pioneer of organised public library development in India under Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III.

Sayajirao considered literacy and education essential to social progress. He believed that formal education alone was insufficient because people also needed opportunities to continue learning after leaving school.

His educational policy therefore connected primary education with access to public libraries. The objective was to develop a reading population capable of acquiring knowledge throughout life.

Development of the library system

The idea of establishing circulating libraries in Baroda emerged in 1901. By 1906, local associations of teachers were organising reading circles and reading rooms in rural communities.

These early initiatives developed into a more systematic state-supported library movement in the following years.

In 1910, Sayajirao brought the American librarian William Alanson Borden to Baroda to assist in organising the public library system. A separate Library Department was established in the same year.

In 1911, Borden received permission to establish training classes for librarians. This helped develop the trained personnel necessary for managing an expanding network of libraries.

Features of the Baroda library system

  • Central Library: A major collection and public reading facility in Baroda that supported the organised library movement.
  • Local libraries: Reading facilities established in towns and villages.
  • Circulating libraries: Collections of books sent to different communities so that readers could access new material.
  • State assistance: Financial and administrative support for developing public library services.
  • Training: Preparation of personnel to manage libraries and encourage reading.

Historical importance

The Baroda experiment demonstrated that library development could become an organised responsibility of the state rather than depend entirely on individual charitable initiatives.

The movement's distinguishing feature was its systematic extension of educational and reading facilities beyond major urban centres. It did not represent the establishment of India's first-ever individual library. Its pioneering significance lay in developing a coordinated public library system.

Prelims focus

  • Princely state associated with the movement: Baroda.
  • Royal patron: Sayajirao Gaekwad III.
  • 1901: Idea of circulating libraries.
  • 1910: Separate Library Department and appointment of W. A. Borden.
  • 1911: Permission for librarian training classes.
  • Trap: Borden was an American library expert, not the ruler who sponsored the movement.

[References: NCERT, Class 10, India and the Contemporary World II, Chapter 7, Print Culture and the Modern World, section Print and the Poor People, p. 174; INFLIBNET Centre, Public Libraries, Pioneers of Public Library Movement in India: Part 1, sections 1.4 and 2; Smt. Hansa Mehta Library, Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda, official Library Chronology, Baroda Library Movement 1901–1918. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Royal patronage and Borden’s professional organisation support Baroda’s library network, extending lifelong learning to readers.
pictures.caption: The Baroda model of organised public library development.

title: Baroda Public Library Movement: Sayajirao Gaekwad III and W. A. Borden

body:
A pioneer of rural reading culture

Motibhai Narsinhbhai Amin (1873–1939) was a Gujarati educationist, social reformer and major contributor to the public library movement in the princely state of Baroda.

He was born at Alindra in Kheda district. His work was based on the belief that education should not remain confined to formal educational institutions and that villages should have access to books and reading facilities.

Motibhai Amin advocated free public libraries that could serve students, adults and other members of rural communities.

Early library initiatives

Vaso library, 1890

In 1890, Motibhai Amin helped establish a library for students at Vaso. This initiative demonstrated his commitment to developing reading habits through local participation and community support.

Mitramandal Pustakalay, Petlad, 1906

In 1906, he established Mitramandal Pustakalay at Petlad. The institution was an important expression of his efforts to make organised reading facilities available beyond the major cities.

Participation in the Baroda library administration

Motibhai Amin was appointed Assistant Curator of Libraries in the Baroda State library administration in 1911. He contributed to the implementation of Sayajirao Gaekwad III's educational and library policies by helping establish and develop libraries in rural areas.

Mobile and circulating libraries

One of Motibhai Amin's important initiatives was the introduction of mobile library services in 1911.

A mobile or circulating library makes books available to communities that do not have sufficient resources for a large permanent collection. In the early Baroda system, books were packed into boxes and sent to different villages.

By circulating collections between communities, the library administration could serve more readers with a limited number of books. The system also helped remote communities gain access to educational material.

Motibhai Amin also encouraged the establishment of children's and women's libraries, the training of library workers and the wider use of reading facilities. His work treated the library as an institution of continuing education rather than merely a place for storing books.

Distinguishing the three principal contributors

The Baroda library movement developed through the cooperation of royal patronage, professional library organisation and local educational initiatives.

  • Sayajirao Gaekwad III: Provided royal patronage, state policy and institutional support.
  • W. A. Borden: Provided professional expertise in library organisation and training.
  • Motibhai Amin: Expanded village libraries, promoted reading habits and implemented circulating library services.

Prelims focus

  • Motibhai Amin: 1873–1939, born at Alindra, Kheda.
  • Vaso student library: 1890.
  • Mitramandal Pustakalay, Petlad: 1906.
  • Assistant Curator of Libraries: 1911.
  • Mobile library initiative: 1911.
  • Trap: Motibhai Amin was the Gujarati educationist associated with rural library expansion; W. A. Borden was the American library expert.

[References: INFLIBNET Centre, Public Libraries, Pioneers of Public Library Movement in India: Part 1, section 3, Motibhai Amin, and subsections 3.1–3.2; Gujarati Vishwakosh, Amin, Motibhai Narsinhbhai; Census of India 2011, District Census Handbook, Kheda, Analytical Note, biographical entry on Motibhai Amin; Smt. Hansa Mehta Library, Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda, Library Chronology, 1901–1918. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Circulating book collections brought reading material closer to rural communities.

title: Motibhai Amin and the Expansion of Village Libraries
